events.c: The instructor asked for a replacement without explaining why. No other unusual behavior was reported.
Five Navy training aircraft left Fort Lauderdale with fourteen people aboard for a navigation exercise.
Practice bombing reportedly ended around 3 p.m. The formation’s exact position then is unknown.
Another instructor heard pilots discussing compass readings and being lost after a turn.
The flight leader reported both compasses unavailable. He believed he was over the Florida Keys, without confirmation.
The base received a report that an aircraft or ship appeared to be lost.
Five aircraft were identified. The leader believed he was south of Florida and west of the Keys.
The leader reported being lost over islands he believed were the Keys, with his compass out.
Another instructor advised flying north toward Miami. This depended on the flight actually being over the Keys.
The leader reported passing a small island with no other land visible. The island remained unidentified.
The leader asked whether radar could locate the formation. Radar did not establish its position.
Rescuers suggested letting an aircraft with a working compass lead. Whether or when leadership changed is unknown.
Another pilot thought flying west would bring the flight to land.
Fading signals led a rescue officer to suspect the Bahamas. He suggested sending an aircraft to establish contact.
The leader reported heading northeast to test whether the flight was over the Gulf of Mexico.
Radio stations were alerted to locate the flight from its signals. Interference delayed the search.
Rescuers requested equipment that could guide the flight toward a radio signal. No reply followed.
An order called for flying east for ten minutes. Whether the flight followed it is unknown.
A waiting rescue aircraft remained grounded, preventing a planned attempt to improve radio contact.
The leader reported that the flight was now heading west.
The leader planned to keep flying west until reaching land or running out of fuel.
Rescuers repeatedly requested a radio frequency change. The leader later declined.
The leader reported weak reception and asked about base weather. The weather reply received no acknowledgment.
The sun set at Fort Lauderdale. Sunset timing at the lost formation’s location is unknown.
The leader asked another aircraft about a possible ship. The reply was unreadable, and no ship was identified.
A failed messaging machine hampered rescue coordination. The message to Banana River went by telephone instead.
Radio signals suggested a broad area within a 100-mile radius. The aircraft’s exact position remained unknown.
Coastal stations were told to maximize lighting. Whether the flight saw those lights is unknown.
The leader declined to change radio frequency because he needed to keep the aircraft together.
A relayed warning said the aircraft might soon need to land on water. No landing was confirmed.
A turn back east was proposed. Whether the flight actually reversed course is unknown.
The estimated search area reached Fort Lauderdale by telephone. It was not broadcast to the missing flight.
A rescue aircraft left Miami to restore radio contact with the flight. The attempt failed.
Rescuers heard unclear conversation between the lost aircraft and recognized one aircraft’s radio identifier.
Radar detected four to six aircraft. They were never identified as Flight 19.
One aircraft called the flight leader without an answer. This was the last logged call.
A Mariner search aircraft left Banana River with thirteen crew members and trainees aboard.
The Mariner sent its departure report. No later communication from it was confirmed.
A tanker saw an apparent explosion and flames, linked to the Mariner’s radar disappearance. The cause remains unknown.
After Flight 19’s last call, a search aircraft encountered low clouds, showers, turbulent air, and rough seas.
The Mariner missed its first hourly position report. A radio operator then tried to contact it.
The tanker’s explosion report arrived. It also described oil on the water and no survivors found.
The rescue duty officer was told the Mariner was overdue and could not be reached.
Search aircraft began leaving Fort Lauderdale at dawn. Searches over sea and land did not find Flight 19.
The inquiry opened in Miami. It later blamed navigation errors and poor judgment, while identifying rescue failures.
The search was to end after the afternoon’s flights. It was closed that night.
The Navy approved the findings and recommended frequent rescue drills to improve coordination.
The Navy rejected blame against the flight leader and concluded the disappearance’s cause was unknown.
The Navy confirmed that the flight leader had been cleared of blame. The cause remained unknown.
A researcher withdrew his identification of an Everglades wreck as Flight 19, attributing it to another accident.
Flight 19 searchers found a Challenger space shuttle fragment in 2022, rather than either missing flight.
By December 2025, no confirmed trace of any of the six aircraft had been found.

numbers.label: Fuel threshold for planned water landing

one_line: Five training aircraft disappeared after navigation trouble; a search aircraft was also lost.
status_why: The final locations and loss sequence remain unknown. The Navy later cleared the flight leader of blame.
